competition: Belgian Mathematical Olympiad (Olympiade Mathématique Belge) - MIDI National Final

problems.problem:
If $x$, $y$ and $z$ are three real numbers such that
$$\begin{cases} x+y+z=0\\ x^2+y^2+z^2=4,\end{cases}$$
what is the value of $x^4+y^4+z^4$?
A rectangular sheet of paper has length $5$ cm. When it is folded so that two opposite vertices are brought onto each other, the length of the fold is $\sqrt{6}$ cm. What is the width of this sheet?

One afternoon, Xavier, Yves and Zoé play table tennis. After each game, the loser gives up his or her place to the one who was not playing. In the evening, Xavier has played $10$ games, Yves $15$ and Zoé $17$.

(a) How many games were played in all?

(b) Who lost the second game?

Let $a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots, a_n$ be $n$ numbers, each equal either to $1$ or to $-1$. For which values of $n$ can the sum
$$a_1a_2+a_2a_3+a_3a_4+\cdots+a_{n-1}a_n+a_na_1$$
be zero? Justify your answer.

Claude forgot to write the multiplication sign between a two-digit number and a three-digit number, and read the whole thing as a single five-digit number; this number is then six times the expected product of the two numbers. What are these two numbers?

Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be three nonzero real numbers such that $a^2+b^2=c^2$. Solve the system
$$\begin{cases} x^2+y^2=z^2\\ (x+a)^2+(y+b)^2=(z+c)^2\end{cases}$$
in the real unknowns $x$, $y$ and $z$ (that is: express in terms of $a$, $b$ and $c$ the set $S$ of triples $(x,y,z)$ of real numbers that satisfy this system).

In a triangle $ABC$, let $D$ (resp. $E$, $F$) be the point of intersection of the side $BC$ (resp. $CA$, $AB$) with the bisector from $A$ (resp. $B$, $C$). Let also $I$ be the common point of the three bisectors. Prove that if
$$\frac{|AI|}{|ID|}=\frac{|BI|}{|IE|}=\frac{|CI|}{|IF|},$$
then triangle $ABC$ is equilateral.

On a circle, twelve distinct points are numbered cyclically from $1$ to $12$. Four tokens bearing the letters $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ occupy, respectively, the points numbered $1$, $2$, $3$ and $4$.

These tokens may move according to the following rule: from one of the numbered points, a token may go to the fifth point in one direction or the other, jumping over four points, provided that the point reached is not occupied by another token.

After a certain number of moves, the four tokens again occupy the places $1$ to $4$, but not necessarily in the order $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$. What are all the permutations that the given rule makes it possible to obtain?

In a school, a chess tournament was organised for the pupils of the 3rd and 4th years; two pupils of the 3rd year took part in it. Each participant played exactly once against each other participant. The winner of each game scored $1$ point and the loser scored none; in case of a draw, each of the two opponents scored $\frac{1}{2}$ point. At the end of the tournament, the pupils of the 3rd year had scored $8$ points together. The pupils of the 4th year all obtained the same whole number of points.

What is this number and how many participants from the 4th year were there? (If several solutions exist, mention them all.)

In the figure below (drawn imprecisely), $AELH$, $BFIE$, $CGJF$ and $DHKG$ are four rectangles of equal area and $IJKL$ is a square. What is the nature of the quadrilateral $ABCD$?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/ombmidi_1998_1_p2_fig.png

When, in an aquarium, two fish of the same species but of different colours meet, they change colour, both of them becoming, at random, one of the other colours that this species can take.

(a) Tetrocampes can be orange, red, green or blue. If an aquarium initially contains $1$ orange tetrocampe, $9$ red tetrocampes, $9$ green tetrocampes and $8$ blue tetrocampes, can the successive meetings lead to all these $27$ tetrocampes becoming the same colour?

(b) Hippodons can be orange, red or blue. If an aquarium initially contains $1$ orange hippodon, $9$ red hippodons and $8$ blue hippodons, can the successive meetings lead to all these $18$ hippodons becoming the same colour?
Prove that if a quadrilateral is inscribed in a circle, then the perpendiculars dropped from the midpoint of each side onto the opposite side are concurrent.

A rectangle whose length is three times its width is covered with a grid of squares. Along each side, four rows of squares are grey; the other squares are white. There are $915$ white squares. How many grey squares are there?

Mathieu wrongly simplifies the fraction $\dfrac{\overline{ab}}{\overline{abc}}$, thus obtaining $\dfrac{\overline{a}}{\overline{ac}}$. And yet, extraordinarily, despite this mistake, the two fractions are equal. What is their common value?

(N.B.: $\overline{abc}$, $\overline{ab}$, etc. denote the numbers formed by juxtaposing the digits $a$, $b$ and $c$; $a$ and $b$; etc.)

In the Yin–Yang figure, the Yin (the black part) and the Yang (the white part) are bounded by semicircles.

(a) Construct a line that divides the Yin as well as the Yang into two parts of equal area.

(b) Are there other solutions? If so, give them. If not, explain why.
Five darts have hit a target in the shape of a disc of radius $10$ cm. Show that at least two of the points of impact are less than $10\sqrt{2}$ cm apart.
On the sides $[AB]$ and $[AD]$ of a parallelogram $ABCD$, the equilateral triangles $ABF$ and $ADE$ are constructed externally. Is triangle $CEF$ always equilateral?
Three nonzero real numbers have the property that each of them is equal to the square of the sum of the other two. What are these three numbers?

Through the vertices $A$ and $B$ of a triangle $ABC$, two lines are drawn so as to divide the interior of the triangle into four regions: three triangles and a quadrilateral. If three of these regions have the same area, show that the quadrilateral is one of them.

Determine all integers $u\le v\le w\le x\le y\le z$ such that
$$2^u+2^v+2^w+2^x+2^y+2^z=2000.$$

The parallelograms $ABCD$ and $AEFG$ are such that $E$ lies on the line $BC$ and $D$ on the line $FG$. Compare the areas of these parallelograms. Are they equal? Is one of them always larger than the other? If so, which one?
Find all integers $x$ for which $\sqrt{x}$ and $\sqrt{x-\sqrt{x}}$ are themselves integers.

Determine all triples $(x,y,z)$ of natural numbers that satisfy the equation
$$\frac{1}{x}+\frac{2}{y}-\frac{3}{z}=1.$$

(a) What are all the values taken by the remainder of the division of $a^3$ by $7$ when $a$ is an arbitrary natural number?

(b) The natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ are such that $a^3+b^3+c^3$ is divisible by $7$. What, then, is the remainder of the division of $a\cdot b\cdot c$ by $7$?

Let $M$ be the midpoint of the base $[AB]$ of an isosceles trapezium $ABCD$ and let $E$ be the point of intersection of $MD$ and $AC$. If $M$ is the centre of the circle circumscribed about the trapezium and if $[AD]$ and $[DE]$ have the same length, determine the measure of the angle $\widehat{DAB}$.
The sum of four real numbers is zero; the sum of their cubes is also zero. Is it true that two of these four numbers are then necessarily opposites of each other?

(a) Do there exist four distinct nonzero natural numbers such that the sum of any three of them is always a prime number?

(b) Do there exist five distinct nonzero natural numbers such that the sum of any three of them is always a prime number?

Let $ABCD$ be a rectangle, $P$ a point located on one of the sides of this rectangle, and $E$ and $F$ the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from $P$ to the diagonals of the rectangle. Prove that the sum $|PE|+|PF|$ remains constant as $P$ runs over the whole perimeter of $ABCD$.

An aquarium has the shape of a rectangular parallelepiped of width $l$, length $L$ and height $h=30$ cm, with $l<h<L$. It is completely filled with water and stands on a horizontal floor. To empty part of its water, if it is tilted about one of the two longer edges of its base until this base makes an angle of $45^\circ$ with the floor, it loses one third of its water; whereas if it is tilted about one of the two shorter edges of its base until this base makes an angle of $45^\circ$ with the floor, it loses four fifths of its water. What is the volume of this aquarium?
The four positive real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ are such that $a>b>c>d$ and $a+b+c+d=1$. Under these conditions, is the inequality $a^2+3b^2+5c^2+7d^2<1$ always valid?
In decimal notation, consider all the numbers with $10$ distinct digits (the leftmost digit being different from $0$). How many of these numbers are divisible by $99\,999$?

Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $|AB|=|AC|$. The bisector of the angle $\widehat{ABC}$ meets the line $AC$ at a point $D$ such that $|BC|=|BD|+|AD|$. Determine the measure in degrees of the angle $\widehat{BAC}$.
Among all the positive integers that are multiples of $2004$, which ones have exactly $20$ positive divisors?

In the parallelogram $ABCD$, the point $M$ is the midpoint of $[BC]$. The point $E$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $D$ to $MA$.

Prove that $|CD|=|CE|$.

$2004$ candles are to be placed on a tiered cake. On the top tier there are $n$ candles, and every other tier has $k$ candles more than the tier immediately above it ($k>0$).

(a) Find the maximum number of tiers of such a cake.

(b) For this maximum number, determine all possible values of the natural numbers $n$ and $k$.

A pack of $2004$ cards is placed in a pile on the table, in an order that we shall call initial. The following operation will be applied to it several times:

Take the card $A$ at the very top and the card $B$ at the very bottom, place $A$ on top of $B$, and then put these two cards back between the $n$-th and the $(n+1)$-th card of the remaining cards of the pack ($1\le n\le 2001$).

This operation is repeated with the same value of $n$, each time taking as $A$ and $B$ the cards then located at the ends of the pack.

(a) Is it certain that the $2004$ cards will at some moment return to the initial order? If so, for the first time after how many operations?

(b) For which value(s) of $n$ will this number of operations be minimal, and for which value(s) of $n$ will it be maximal?
What are all the lists of consecutive natural numbers whose sum is $2005$?

On a rectangular billiard table $ABCD$, a ball is shot from the corner $A$; it bounces according to the laws of reflection on the side $CD$, then on the side $BC$, then on the side $BA$, and ends its course in the corner $D$. What is the length of the path of the centre of the ball, given that the diameter of the ball is $6$ cm and that the dimensions of the billiard table are $|AD|=|BC|=156$ cm and $|AB|=|CD|=306$ cm?

The final of a mathematical competition consists of four problems. For each of the problems the possible marks are $0$, $1$, $2$, $3$ and $4$ points. After the competition, the jury notices that for any pair of participants, these two participants did not obtain the same number of points on more than one problem. What is the maximum number of participants?

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral having no right angle and whose four vertices lie on the same circle. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from $D$ to $AB$ and $BC$ respectively. Let $R$ and $S$ be the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from $B$ to $AD$ and $CD$ respectively. The convex quadrilateral formed by the four points $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$:

(a) Is it necessarily a trapezium?

(b) Does it necessarily have two equal sides?

Through the vertex $A$ of triangle $ABC$, a line $d$ is drawn. The feet of the perpendiculars dropped from $B$ and from $C$ to $d$ are $D$ and $E$ respectively. If $M$ is the midpoint of $[BC]$, prove that $|MD|=|ME|$.

In the table below, each cell is identified by its row number and its column number. Row $1$ starts with $2006$, and to go from the number written in column $k$ to the number written in column $k+1$ one subtracts $1$. Row $2$ starts with $2005$ and one subtracts $2$ each time. Row $3$ starts with $2004$ and one subtracts $3$ each time. And so on.
$$\begin{array}{c||c|c|c|c|c|c}
 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & \cdots\\ \hline\hline
1 & 2006 & 2005 & 2004 & 2003 & 2002 & \cdots\\ \hline
2 & 2005 & 2003 & 2001 & 1999 & 1997 & \cdots\\ \hline
3 & 2004 & 2001 & 1998 & 1995 & \cdots & \\ \hline
4 & 2003 & 1999 & 1995 & 1991 & \cdots & \\ \hline
5 & 2002 & 1997 & 1992 & \cdots & & \\ \hline
\cdots & \cdots & & & & &
\end{array}$$

(a) What is the number written in row $10$, column $20$?

(b) In which cells does the number $0$ appear? Explain your answer.

(c) If the number in row $1$, column $1$ of the table is $n$, how can one determine, in terms of $n$, the cells in which the number $0$ appears?

Three numbers whose product is $1$ are such that their sum is equal to the sum of their reciprocals.

(a) Give a numerical example in which the three numbers are different.

(b) Is it true that at least one of the numbers is always equal to $1$? If so, prove it; if not, give a counterexample.

On the target shown below, there are only two regions, one worth $4$ points (the outer ring) and the other worth $9$ points (the inner disc). When several arrows are shot one after another, the score is the sum of the points scored in the regions where the arrows landed.

(a) Are there natural numbers that cannot be obtained as scores? Which is the largest of them, if it exists?

(b) Some natural numbers can be obtained as scores in at least two different ways. What is the smallest number from which on all the following scores can be obtained in at least two ways?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/ombmidi_2006_1_p4_fig.png

The units digit of the natural number $N$ is $x$. The following operations are carried out in succession:

– delete the units digit $x$ of the number $N$;

– subtract $2x$ from the number obtained.

For example, the number $203$ becomes $20$, then $14$.

Is it always true that the final number is a multiple of $7$ if and only if the initial number $N$ is a multiple of $7$?

(a) Find all pairs of positive integers whose sum is equal to their product. Prove that there are no others.

(b) Find all triples of positive integers forming an arithmetic sequence whose sum is equal to their product. Prove that there are no others.

(The sequence $(a,b,c)$ is called an arithmetic sequence when there exists an integer $r$ such that $(a,b,c)=(a,a+r,a+2r)$.)

(c) What becomes of the answer to part (b) if the arithmetic sequence is formed of arbitrary integers (positive, negative or zero)?

Triangle $ABC$ is right-angled, with $\widehat{ABC}$ measuring $90^\circ$. The foot of the altitude to the hypotenuse is $D$, and the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from $D$ to $[BA]$ and $[BC]$ are $E$ and $F$ respectively. Let $r_1$, $r_2$ and $r_3$ be the radii of the circles inscribed in the triangles $AED$, $EDF$ and $FDC$ respectively. Is the formula $r_2=\sqrt{r_1\cdot r_3}$ always correct?

In the plane, how many distinct equilateral triangles are there at least two of whose vertices are also vertices

(a) of a given square?

(b) of a given regular hexagon?

(c) of a given regular dodecagon (polygon with $12$ vertices)?

Consider $2008$ fractions
$$\frac{a_1}{b_1},\ \frac{a_2}{b_2},\ \frac{a_3}{b_3},\ \ldots,\ \frac{a_{2008}}{b_{2008}}$$
whose numerators are natural numbers and whose denominators are nonzero natural numbers. Prove that if $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are respectively the smallest and the largest of these fractions, then
$$\alpha\leqslant\frac{a_1+a_2+a_3+\cdots+a_{2008}}{b_1+b_2+b_3+\cdots+b_{2008}}\leqslant\beta.$$

Triangle $ABC$ is inscribed in a circle with centre $O$. The altitude from $A$ meets $BC$ at $H$. The circle with diameter $[AH]$ meets $AB$ at $D$ and meets $AC$ at $E$. Prove that $OA$ is perpendicular to $DE$.

The dimensions of a rectangular plot of land are expressed by two natural numbers $x$ and $y$. The owner has the possibility of enlarging his plot so that it remains rectangular, but its dimensions are now $x+5$ and $y+6$. He notices that after this enlargement the area of his plot has tripled. What are all the possible values of $x$ and $y$?

Let $n$ be a natural number. Denote by $P_n$ the property "$n^2-1$ is a multiple of $12$".

(a) Show that $P_n$ is true if $n$ is a prime number other than $2$ or $3$.

(b) Give an example of a composite number $n$ for which $P_n$ is true and another for which $P_n$ is false.

(c) If $n$ is composite, under what condition on $n$ is the property $P_n$ true?

Two right triangles $ABC$ and $ABD$ lie on the same side of their common hypotenuse $[AB]$. Their sides $AC$ and $BD$ meet at $I$. Let $H$ be the orthogonal projection of $I$ onto $AB$. Show that $IH$ is the bisector of $\widehat{CHD}$.

Mathilde has $n$ identical candles. Every Sunday she lights one or more candles for exactly one hour: on the first Sunday, one candle; on the second, two candles; and so on up to the $n$-th Sunday, on which she lights the $n$ candles. On that Sunday, at the end of the hour, the $n$ candles are completely burnt out.

(a) Is this possible when $n=9$ (if the burning times of the candles are suitable)?

(b) Is this possible when $n=10$ (if the burning times of the candles are suitable)?

(c) Determine all values of $n$ for which this is possible (if the burning times of the candles are suitable). Explain how to proceed.

A farmer owns a square meadow of side $30$ m, fenced along its whole perimeter. He wishes to divide it into three plots of equal area. For this he has $50$ m of fencing (which he is not obliged to use entirely).

(a) Is such a division possible?

(b) Is it possible in several non-isometric ways?

Let $ABCD$ be a square. On the sides $[AB]$, $[BC]$, $[CD]$ and $[DA]$, the points $A'$, $B'$, $C'$ and $D'$ are constructed so that $|AA'|=|BB'|=|CC'|=|DD'|$. Show that, whatever the point $P$ chosen inside the square,
$$\mathcal{A}(AA'PD')+\mathcal{A}(CC'PB')=\mathcal{A}(BB'PA')+\mathcal{A}(DD'PC').$$
($\mathcal{A}(F)$ denotes the area of the figure $F$.)
Determine all natural numbers $n$ that are perfect squares and such that $n=7p+4$, where $p$ is a prime number.

Let $m$ and $n$ be two natural numbers such that the decimal representation of $n$ is obtained by permuting the digits of the decimal representation of $m$.

(a) Is the sum of the digits of $2m$ the same as that of $2n$?

(b) Is the sum of the digits of $3m$ the same as that of $3n$?

(c) Is the sum of the digits of $5m$ the same as that of $5n$?

(d) If $n$ and $m$ are even, is the sum of the digits of $m/2$ the same as that of $n/2$?
Let $ABCD$ be a square with centre $E$. The line $CF$ is tangent to the circle with diameter $AB$ at $F\neq B$. What is the ratio of the areas of triangle $BEF$ and of the square $ABCD$?
Let $C_1$, $C_2$ and $C_3$ be three circles of the same radius $r$, pairwise tangent. How many circles are there that are tangent to these three circles? What are their radii?
Determine all pairs $(x,y)$ of integers such that $\dfrac{1}{x}+\dfrac{1}{y}=\dfrac{1}{2011}$.

Let $a$ and $b$ be two nonzero real numbers with strictly positive sum. Show that
$$\frac{a}{b^2}+\frac{b}{a^2}\geqslant\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}$$
and determine in which cases it is true that
$$\frac{a}{b^2}+\frac{b}{a^2}=\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}.$$

In a triangle $ABC$, the bisector of the angle $B$ meets $[AC]$ at $D$. The circle circumscribed about triangle $ADB$ meets $[BC]$ at $F$ and the circle circumscribed about triangle $BDC$ meets $[AB]$ at $E$. Prove that $|AE|=|CF|$.

Let $a$ and $b$ be integers that differ by a multiple of $3$.

(a) Is the number $\frac{2}{3}(a^2+ab+b^2)$ always a sum of two squares of integers?

(b) Is it always a sum of three squares of integers?

Augustin, Bérénice, Coralie and Damien choose numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$, not necessarily distinct, and then tell them to one another. They notice that the numbers of choices of $0$, of $1$, of $2$ and of $3$ are exactly $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ (but not necessarily in this order). What are all the lists $(a,b,c,d)$ compatible with this information?

A hexagon $ABCDEF$ is called "sympa" if it is inscribed in a circle and the bisectors of the angles $\widehat{ABC}$, $\widehat{CDE}$ and $\widehat{EFA}$ all three pass through the centre $O$ of this circle.

(a) Prove that if $ABCDEF$ is sympa, then $\widehat{AOB}=\widehat{BOC}$.

(b) Are there non-regular sympa hexagons? If so, construct a figure showing one. (Explain the construction carried out.)

(c) Prove that the three long diagonals $[AD]$, $[BE]$ and $[CF]$ of a sympa hexagon are concurrent.

(d) Let $B$, $D$ and $F$ be three non-collinear points. Construct (with "ruler and compass") three points $A$, $C$ and $E$ such that the hexagon $ABCDEF$ is sympa.

The lengths of the three sides of an isosceles triangle are $29$, $29$ and $40$ respectively.

(a) Compute its perimeter and its area.

(b) Is there an isosceles triangle having the same perimeter and the same area, although the lengths of its sides are different from those of the previous triangle? If so, give all the isosceles triangles that satisfy this.

(a) A test consists of $5$ questions, marked out of $10$, $10$, $35$, $25$ and $20$ points respectively. (The maximum total is thus $100$ points.) The teacher marks these questions in order.

i. A pupil obtained $5$, $3$ and $10$ on the first three questions. Is it still possible for him to have at least $50$ in total?

ii. At the end of the marking of these first three questions, what partial total must a pupil have obtained at least in order still to be able to hope that his final total will be at least $50$? And at the end of the marking of the first $k$ questions ($k=1,2,4$)?

(b) A test consists of $n$ questions, marked out of $m_1,\ldots,m_n$ points respectively. (The maximum total is thus $m=m_1+\cdots+m_n$.) The teacher marks these questions in order. At the end of the marking of the first $k$ questions ($1\leqslant k<n$), what partial total must a pupil have obtained at least in order still to be able to hope that his final total will be at least $m/2$?

(a) Give two examples in which the difference of the squares of two odd numbers is divisible by $8$.

(b) Is the difference of the squares of two odd numbers $a$ and $b$ always divisible by $8$? Justify.

(c) Give an example in which the difference of the cubes of two odd numbers is divisible by $8$.

(d) Is the difference of the cubes of two odd numbers $a$ and $b$ always divisible by $8$? If not, give a condition on $a$ and $b$ for it to be so.

(a) Let $S$ be the sum of the integers from $1$ to $20$ and $S'$ the sum of the integers from $21$ to $40$. What is $S'-S$?

(b) And what is $T'-T$ if $T=1+2+\cdots+2013$ and $T'=2014+2015+\cdots+4026$?

(c) If $N=1+2+\cdots+n$ and $N'=(n+1)+(n+2)+\cdots+2n$, is it true that $N'-N$ is a perfect square for every nonzero natural number $n$?

(d) Let $k\geqslant 2$ be a natural number. If $N=1+2+\cdots+n$ and $N_k=(n+1)+(n+2)+\cdots+kn$ (with $n$ a nonzero natural number), establish a formula expressing $N_k$ in terms of $N$, $n$ and $k$. Is it true that $N_k-N$ is a perfect square for every $n$?

(a) The Reuleaux triangle, constructed from an equilateral triangle, is the union of three circular arcs of $60^\circ$ (see the left-hand figure). Show that its width is the same in every direction (see the centre figure).

(b) We wish to form other curves of constant width, starting from a triangle $ABC$ whose sides measure $a=3$, $b=4$ and $c=2$, by drawing six circular arcs as in the right-hand figure: each side of the triangle is extended in both directions; each vertex becomes the centre of two circular arcs "on either side", whose radii, for example around $A$, are $x$ and $b+z$.

i. For these values of $a$, $b$ and $c$, show that there exists at least one choice of values of $x$, $y$ and $z$ that gives a continuous curve.

ii. For these values of $a$, $b$ and $c$, what are all the choices of values for $x$, $y$ and $z$ that give a continuous curve?

iii. What is the perimeter of the continuous figure thus drawn? Show that its width is the same in every direction.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/ombmidi_2013_1_p4_fig.png

The lines $d_1$ and $d_2$ are externally tangent to two circles of distinct radii, while $d$ is internally tangent to them. The line $d$ is tangent to the circles at $A$ and $B$, the line $d_1$ at $A_1$ and $B_1$, and the line $d_2$ at $A_2$ and $B_2$. The line $d$ meets $d_1$ at $X$ and $d_2$ at $Y$ (see the figure).

(a) Suppose first that, in addition, the two circles are tangent to each other.

i. Adapt the figure to this particular case.

ii. Then express $|A_1B_1|$ in terms of the radii of the two circles.

(b) In the general case, prove that

i. $|A_1B_1|=|A_2B_2|$;

ii. $|A_1B_1|=|XY|$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/ombmidi_2014_1_p1_fig.png

Consider the system
$$\begin{cases} x^2+y^2+z^2=2(xy+4)\\ x+y+z=2014,\end{cases}$$
in which $x$, $y$ and $z$ are integers.

(a) Solve it, with respect to the unknowns $x$ and $y$, when $z=2$.

(b) Solve it, with respect to the unknowns $x$ and $y$, when $z=0$.

(c) Solve it in general, with respect to the unknowns $x$, $y$ and $z$.

Let $m$, $n$ be two nonzero natural numbers. A hexagon is constructed whose angles are $120^\circ$ and whose sides measure alternately $m$ and $n$. This hexagon is tiled by equilateral triangles of side $1$, and all the vertices of these triangles are marked (see the figure).

(a) How many points have been marked when $m=20$ and $n=14$?

(b) How many points have been marked in the general case?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/ombmidi_2014_1_p3_fig.png

In a class of $n$ pupils, friendship is symmetric: if $A$ is a friend of $B$, then $B$ is a friend of $A$; moreover, $A$ is not considered a friend of $A$. Is it always true that:

(a) If $n\geqslant 2$, at least two pupils have the same number of friends?

(b) The number of pupils having an even number of friends is odd?

(c) The number of pupils having an odd number of friends is even?

(d) If every pupil has at least two friends, then there exists a pupil $A$ who is a friend of a friend of a friend$\ldots$ of a friend of $A$ himself, the friends involved in this chain other than $A$, all distinct, numbering at least $2$?

(e) If there are strictly more than $(n-1)(n-2)/2$ pairs of friends in the class, then for any two distinct pupils $A$ and $B$, $A$ is a friend of a friend of a friend$\ldots$ of a friend of $B$, the number of friends involved in this chain other than $A$ and $B$ being at least $0$?
